title: Humidifier (ultrasonic, evaporative, warm mist or steam): safe teardown
summary: Get the water tank, the fan, the plug-in power supply, the ultrasonic mist driver with its disc, the low-water float and, in warm-mist models, the heater out of a household humidifier. The dangers are mains electricity near water, scalding water in warm-mist and steam models, and mould and bacteria growing in the tank and wick.

steps.text: Unplug it, or unplug its adapter from the wall, and keep the plug where you can see it. Warm-mist and steam models: leave them at least 30 minutes to cool. Vicks says to wait at least 15 minutes before lifting off the tank or cooling chamber of its V745A, and 20–30 minutes before handling its V150 vaporizer (Vicks V745A manual, Vicks V150 manual).
steps.warn: Hot water and steam can scald. Never lift a tank or chamber off a unit that has just been running.

steps.text: Take it outdoors. Put on gloves, goggles and an N95 or P2 mask. Pour the water out of the tank and the base well, away from any water you drink, then stand the base upside down to drain and dry. Don't put the base under water (Levoit Classic 160 manual).
steps.warn: A tank left standing can grow bacteria and mould, and ultrasonic and impeller types spray what grows into the air (EPA humidifiers). Don't breathe spray from a dirty tank.

steps.text: Work out which type it is. A disc in the bottom of the water well is ultrasonic (Levoit calls it the transducer). A wick with a fan is evaporative. A heating chamber is warm mist; some models, like the Levoit LV600HH, have both a heater and a transducer (Levoit LV600HH manual). A steam vaporizer whose maker says to add salt if it won't steam, like the Vicks V150, has an electrode heating unit (Vicks V150 manual).
steps.warn: Electrode units heat water by passing mains current through it (Resideo electrode steam manual). Leave the steam unit whole and never plug it in: Vicks warns against taking it apart (Vicks V150 manual). Take only the cord.

steps.text: If it came with a remote, take out the remote's coin cell (a CR2025 in the LV600HH: Levoit LV600HH manual) and put it straight into a closed container.
steps.warn: A coin cell swallowed by a child can burn through the throat in as little as two hours (CPSC Reese's Law). Keep cells away from children, and get a child to emergency care at once if one is swallowed.

steps.text: Once the base is dry, turn it over on a towel and undo the base screws. Some hide under feet or labels; some need security bits. Lift the cover off, but don't touch any wire yet.

Wait at least 5 minutes since you unplugged it. Check your meter on a battery. Find any capacitors on the boards (a model with a mains cord and a circuit board has a supply inside). Discharge each one rated over 50 V, or with no readable rating, with a resistor tool, measure DC volts across it, then check the meter on the battery again. Under 1 V is safe; clip a wire across any big capacitor and leave it there (see safety_discharge_capacitor).
steps.warn: Never measure first, and never short a capacitor with a screwdriver.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring. Unplug the fan, pump and sensor leads at their connectors. Lift out the mist driver board whole, with the transducer's wires still on it. One maker's design drives the disc from a power transistor and a coil (EFY Holtek humidifier).

Free the transducer disc from the floor of the water well: undo the ring or screws that hold it and keep any rubber seal. Hold the disc by its edge and don't scratch its face. Keep it wired to its board: it does nothing without its driver.

Take out the low-water float: lift one end and slide its shaft out of the brackets (Levoit Classic 160 manual). If the float has a small magnet in it, look under the well for a glass reed switch on two wires and take it with its wires.
steps.warn: Reed switches are thin glass. Don't bend the leads close to the glass.

steps.text: Take the fan, and the pump if it has one (the Levoit Superior 6000S has a water pump tube on its wick frame: Levoit 6000S manual). Undo their screws, read their labels and write the volts on them.

Warm-mist models: first check the heater is cold. In a very old unit, look at what the heater sits on: grey or white fibrous board or papery wrap may be asbestos, so stop and leave it (see safety_asbestos_check). Otherwise unscrew the heater with its cut-outs. Cut each cut-out's leads as far from its body as you can. Never heat a cut-out and never bridge one with wire.
Cut the cord off at the case, leaving it long. Keep a plug-in adapter whole and read its label: the Levoit Superior 6000S runs from 24 V, 1.25 A (Levoit 6000S manual).

If you keep the tank, scrub it, clean it with the maker's cleaner, or 3% hydrogen peroxide if you have no maker's instructions, rinse it well and dry it fully (EPA humidifiers). Then test the other parts (see the notes) and label them OK or BAD.
steps.warn: Never mix bleach with vinegar, ammonia or other cleaners: it gives off toxic gas. Never mix hydrogen peroxide with vinegar either (Levoit LV600HH manual).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Water tank.** A clean, lidded container. The Levoit LV600HH's holds 6 L (Levoit LV600HH manual) and the Superior 6000S's 22.7 L (Levoit 6000S manual). Good for carrying and storing washing water. Clean and dry it first (EPA humidifiers). Don't count on it for drinking water unless the plastic is marked food-safe.
- **Fan.** The Superior 6000S runs its fan and pump from a 24 V adapter (Levoit 6000S manual); in one maker's reference design the fan draws only about 1 W (EFY Holtek humidifier). A small low-voltage fan cools electronics, dries food on a rack, or vents a small space. Read the voltage on its label before you power it.
- **Plug-in adapter.** The 6000S adapter gives 24 V, 1.25 A (Levoit 6000S manual): enough for LED lighting or a small pump. Keep it whole; don't open it.
- **Mist driver and transducer.** The disc vibrates at high frequency to make a cool mist (EPA humidifiers). One maker's reference design is labelled 1.7 MHz, 24 V and 20 W, with about 17 W going to the atomizer film, and its power transistor reached 63 °C in testing (EFY Holtek humidifier), so expect a driver board's transistor to run warm. The Levoit Classic 160 says its humidifier complies with FCC Part 18, the rules for equipment that makes radio-frequency energy for non-radio uses (Levoit Classic 160 manual), so keep it away from radios. A working pair makes a mist maker, for example to keep seedlings or cuttings damp. Run it only with water over the disc, as the humidifier itself does: the Levoit stops misting when its tank is empty (Levoit Classic 160 manual).
- **Float and reed switch.** A ready water-level sensor for a tank alarm or pump control. Use it on low voltage only.
- **Heater (warm-mist models).** The LV600HH is rated 280 W on 220–240 V in all (Levoit LV600HH manual). A small mains heater built to heat water. Use it only at its own voltage, earthed, through an RCD (GFCI), with its terminals covered and kept out of the water, and never run it dry.
- **Cut-outs.** The V745A's heater switches itself off when the water is nearly used up (Vicks V745A manual). If you find a cut-out on a heater, a continuity reading doesn't prove a salvaged one will still trip. Never heat one to test it, never bridge one, and never make a salvaged one the only protection.
- **Cord and plug.** Keep a cord with whole insulation and its plug, for repairs (see repair_extension_cord).
- **Remote's coin cell.** A CR2025 in the LV600HH remote (Levoit LV600HH manual). A coin cell swallowed by a child can burn through the throat in as little as two hours (CPSC Reese's Law), so keep it in a closed jar away from children.

## Testing what you got out

- **Adapter.** Look over the case, pins and cord first: cracks, scorch marks, corrosion or a damaged cord mean scrap it, because it has sat next to water. If it looks sound, plug it in through an RCD (GFCI), keep the probes clear of the pins, and measure the output: within about 5% of the label is good.
- **Fan and pump.** Feed the voltage on the label from a bench supply (30 V or less), fan clear of fingers.
- **Heater.** Wires off, measure ohms: about volts × volts ÷ watts from its label. OL means burnt out. From each terminal to the metal body must read OL.
- **Reed switch.** Meter on continuity: it should close when the float's magnet comes near.
- **Transducer.** There is no simple meter test. Try it only on a driver board fed from a supply of 30 V or less, with the board dry and above the water and the disc under water. If the board's label shows more than 30 V, don't test it. Never test a mains-fed board outside its case.

## Variations

- **Ultrasonic (Levoit Classic 160).** 120 V, 60 Hz, 17 W; a transducer, a float and a secondary float in the base. With no water in the tank it stops misting and lights a refill lamp (Levoit Classic 160 manual). Ultrasonic and impeller types throw minerals and microbes from the tank into the air (EPA humidifiers).
- **Evaporative (Levoit Superior 6000S).** A fan pushes air through damp wicks (EPA humidifiers). The 6000S runs from a 24 V, 1.25 A adapter at 30 W and lifts water to its wicks through a pump tube. Its wicks come wrapped in plastic, which must be taken off before use or it may overheat (Levoit 6000S manual).
- **Hybrid (Levoit LV600HH).** Ultrasonic transducer plus a heating element; 220–240 V, 280 W; the water stays warm after it is switched off (Levoit LV600HH manual).
- **Warm mist (Vicks V745A).** A heater in a heating chamber on 120 V. Scale from tap water builds up on the heater and helps microbes grow; Vicks descales it with vinegar (Vicks V745A manual).
- **Steam vaporizer (Vicks V150).** An electrode heating unit makes the steam, and in soft-water areas it needs a pinch of salt to make steam (Vicks V150 manual). Electrode units pass mains current through the water (Resideo electrode steam manual), so never run or test the steam unit. Take only the cord.

## What to leave

- An electrode vaporizer's steam unit (Vicks V150 manual).
- Wicks, foam filters and anything slimy or mouldy: bag them and bin them.
- Heaters thick with scale or with cracked sheaths.
- Cracked tanks.
